summary: This standards-track memo supplements RFC 3279. It describes how to use the RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm, the RSAES-OAEP key transport algorithm, and additional hash functions in X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists.

eli5.summary: Digital certificates use maths to prove who is who. This document adds newer, safer ways to do that maths with RSA.

subtitle: How certificates and CRLs identify RSA-PSS signatures, RSA-OAEP keys and SHA-2 hashes.

tldr.problem: RFC 3279 covered only older RSA conventions for X.509 certificates and CRLs. There was no way to say that a key is meant only for the RSASSA-PSS signature scheme or the RSAES-OAEP key transport scheme, and no identifiers for the SHA-2 hashes with PKCS #1 v1.5.
tldr.mechanism: It defines algorithm identifiers and parameter structures for RSASSA-PSS and RSAES-OAEP public keys and signatures. It also defines identifiers for SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 with the PKCS #1 version 1.5 signature algorithm.
tldr.outcome: A certificate can now say that its RSA key may be used only for PSS signatures or only for OAEP key transport, along with the exact hash and mask function. It updates RFC 3279 and has itself been updated by RFC 5756.

facts.label: Required RSA key size
facts.value: 1024 bits supported; 2048 SHOULD by end of 2007

today: RFC 4055 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3279. It has itself been updated by RFC 5756. It is not marked as obsoleted in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This document supplements RFC 3279 and the Internet X.509 certificate and CRL profile (RFC 3280). It describes how to use two RSA-based algorithms from PKCS #1 version 2.1, RSASSA-PSS (a signature scheme) and RSAES-OAEP (a key transport scheme), in certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs).

It specifies the algorithm identifiers and parameters for subject public keys that use either algorithm, and the encoding of RSASSA-PSS signatures. It also adds identifiers for using SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 with the older PKCS #1 version 1.5 signature algorithm. For each algorithm it says which keyUsage values are appropriate.
sections.eli5: Certificates are like ID cards. This RFC adds new, stronger ways to sign them and new labels that say what a key is allowed to do.

sections.title: Marking an RSA Public Key
sections.content:
Traditionally the rsaEncryption object identifier marks an RSA public key. It stays in use when the key owner does not want to limit the key to one scheme. In that case its parameters field MUST be NULL.

When the owner wants to limit the key exclusively to RSASSA-PSS, the id-RSASSA-PSS identifier MUST be used. For RSAES-OAEP only, id-RSAES-OAEP MUST be used. A key cannot be restricted to a set of both algorithms. In every case the key itself is encoded the same way, as an RSAPublicKey holding the modulus n and the public exponent e.

The keyUsage extension can show the intended use. For a PSS key in an end-entity certificate it MUST contain nonRepudiation, digitalSignature or both. For a CA certificate it MUST contain one or more of those plus keyCertSign and cRLSign. For an OAEP key it MUST contain only keyEncipherment and dataEncipherment, and both SHOULD NOT be present together.

A restricted key MUST be used only for the matching operations, with the hash and mask functions named in the key's parameters, if present.
sections.eli5: A normal key is like a master key that opens anything. A restricted key has a label saying 'only for signing' or 'only for sealing secrets', and everyone must respect the label.

sections.title: Hash and Mask Generation Functions
sections.content:
Both new schemes use a one-way hash function and a mask generation function. The hashes are SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, each with its own object identifier. SHA-224 is what this document adds to the four that PKCS #1 version 2.1 already supported. No other hash functions are supported by this specification. The only mask generation function is MGF1, whose parameters name the hash it uses.

Implementations MUST support SHA-1 and MAY support the others, both for hashing and for MGF1.

The identifiers for the hashes have a history. The correct encoding omits the parameters field, but RSASSA-PSS and RSAES-OAEP were defined with NULL parameters. So all implementations MUST accept both NULL and absent parameters as legal and equivalent.
sections.eli5: A hash is a fingerprint-maker for data. The RFC lists which fingerprint-makers are allowed and says to accept two different ways of writing the same label.

sections.title: RSASSA-PSS Signatures
sections.content:
When id-RSASSA-PSS appears in an algorithm identifier, the parameters MUST use the RSASSA-PSS-params syntax. They may be absent in a subject public key, but MUST be present in the identifier attached to a signature. The structure has four fields, each with a default.

  • hashAlgorithm: default SHA-1. A signer MUST omit it when SHA-1 is used.
  • maskGenAlgorithm: default MGF1 with SHA-1. It is strongly RECOMMENDED that MGF1 use the same hash as hashAlgorithm.
  • saltLength: octet length of the salt, default 20. The recommended value is the number of octets in the hash value. Unlike the other fields it may vary from signature to signature.
  • trailerField: default 1, which means the trailer byte 0xBC. No other value is supported.

CAs that sign with RSASSA-PSS MUST include the parameters in the signature algorithm field of what they sign, and SHOULD include them in their own certificates' public key information. Validators MUST support SHA-1.

The signature value is an octet string as long as the modulus. In certificates and CRLs it is converted to a bit string, with the most significant bit of the first octet becoming the first bit.

When parameters are present in both key and signature, all must match except saltLength, and the signature's value MUST be greater than or equal to the key's.
sections.eli5: A signature recipe has settings: which fingerprint-maker, which scrambler, how much random salt, and a closing mark. If the certificate lists the settings, every signature has to follow them.

sections.title: RSAES-OAEP Key Transport
sections.content:
RSAES-OAEP is used to send a secret key encrypted to the holder of an RSA key. Conforming CAs and applications MUST support it with SHA-1, and the other four hashes MAY be supported. CAs SHOULD require parameters in certificates that carry id-RSAES-OAEP.

The RSAES-OAEP-params structure has three fields, each with a default:

  • hashFunc: default SHA-1.
  • maskGenFunc: default MGF1 with SHA-1. Using the same hash as hashFunc is strongly RECOMMENDED.
  • pSourceFunc: the source of the encoding parameter P. It MUST be id-pSpecified, and the default P is an empty string. Implementations MUST support a zero length P.

As with PSS, a party doing encryption MUST omit a field when its default is used. A party doing decryption MUST accept either the default's explicit form or its absence.
sections.eli5: OAEP is a way to wrap a secret key in a padded, scrambled package before locking it with RSA. The settings say how to scramble it, and the defaults are fine unless the certificate says otherwise.

sections.title: SHA-2 with PKCS #1 Version 1.5
sections.content:
The older PKCS #1 version 1.5 signature algorithm (RFC 2313) was used in RFC 3279 with MD2, MD5 and SHA-1. This document adds identifiers for SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512: sha224WithRSAEncryption, sha256WithRSAEncryption, sha384WithRSAEncryption and sha512WithRSAEncryption. The data encoding step MUST use the matching id-sha224, id-sha256, id-sha384 or id-sha512 identifiers.

The RFC prefers RSASSA-PSS. Although no attacks are known against the version 1.5 algorithm, PSS is recommended for eventual adoption, especially by new applications. A gradual transition is encouraged.
sections.eli5: The old way of signing still works and now has labels for the newer fingerprint-makers. But the RFC says to move slowly toward the new way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says to protect the RSA private key and to generate keys with a good random number generator. It advises using a given RSA key pair in only one scheme. A PSS signing key should not be used for other purposes and should keep the same parameters, except possibly salt length. An OAEP key likewise.

SHA-1 must be supported for interoperability. The RFC notes a collision attack against SHA-1 with complexity 2^69, compared with a generic attack of 2^80. Thus SHA-1 in a signature scheme gives a security level of no more than 69 bits if an attacker can get a signer to sign a colliding message. For more security it points to SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. A 1024-bit RSA key is considered to give about 80 bits of security.

Current implementations MUST support 1024-bit RSA public keys. Before the end of 2007, implementations SHOULD support RSA keys of at least 2048 bits and SHOULD support SHA-256.
sections.eli5: An old fingerprint-maker has been found to have weak spots, and short keys are easier to crack. So the RFC says to start using longer keys and stronger fingerprint-makers, and to use each key for just one job.
